sources.entry: A proxy is a server application that acts as an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing that resource. This section about forward (i.e. outgoing) proxies. For reverse proxies, see the Web Server section.

summary.name: Proxy server
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article explaining proxy servers: intermediaries that forward client requests to other servers, covering forward, reverse, open, caching, transparent and CGI proxies.
use_cases: Understanding how forward and reverse proxies differ
Setting up content filtering in an organization
Caching web content to reduce bandwidth
Choosing web proxy software such as Squid or Nginx
Evaluating privacy and logging risks of proxies
summary.what_it_does: The page defines a proxy server as an intermediary that receives a client's resource request and performs the network transaction on the client's behalf. It distinguishes forward proxies (outgoing, used for filtering, masking and policy) from reverse proxies (in front of servers, used for TLS termination, load balancing, caching and security). It describes uses such as content filtering, caching, censorship circumvention, geotargeted ad testing and NAT-based security. It also covers implementation details including HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS, transparent interception, and detection methods, and lists example software such as Apache, HAProxy, Nginx, Squid, Privoxy and Varnish.
notable: Covers forward, reverse, transparent and CGI proxy types in one reference
Lists web proxy server implementations and client OS/browser support
Explains privacy, logging and encrypted-traffic filtering trade-offs
caveats: Page notes it needs more citations
Forwarding headers like X-Forwarded-For are not inherently trustworthy
Web filtering proxies cannot inspect encrypted traffic without a trusted root certificate
